Here the domain requires back-to-back bookings to remain distinguishable, so equality starts a new output interval. The merge implementation must therefore use the same strict comparator as conflict detection. The transfer boundary matters: if the output contract cares only about covered measure and not booking boundaries, coalescing adjacency could be valid, but it would be a different declared normalization policy.

blocks.text: The counterexample [2, 3), [4, 5), [1, 10) in end order shows the problem. After the first two intervals are emitted separately, [1, 10) overlaps both but arrives too late to revise the first output. Start sorting would place the containing interval first and preserve one active union component. The lesson is not that end sorting is generally bad; it is that a one-pass union merge needs the exact monotonic boundary supplied by start order. Finish-time order belongs to different objectives with different proofs.

blocks.text: These invariants divide committed state from mutable state. Emitted intervals lie strictly before the active interval and cannot be affected by unseen starts. The active interval begins at the first start of the current component and ends at the maximum end encountered in that component. Comparing the next interval against this summary captures transitive overlap chains. If the active interval could begin before emitted output, or if its end tracked only the latest input, prior emission would be unsafe and containment would lose coverage. The invariants are the correctness argument behind the concise implementation.

blocks.text: A direct start-sorted merge is simpler for this batch, but an event representation can reconstruct the same policy only if its equal-time transitions are defined. For [1, 3) and [3, 5), processing the end at 3 closes the first range before the start opens the second. Processing start first keeps active positive and produces one combined range. If the product instead wanted pure set-union compression, joining adjacent ranges could be acceptable, but the change must be explicit. The event tie is therefore part of semantic equivalence, not a sorting implementation detail.

blocks.text: The in-place heapsort costs O(n log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space under the explicit algorithm stated in the prompt. The subsequent merge scan examines every interval once and keeps only the active interval plus loop state, so it adds O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Total time is therefore O(n log n), and extra space remains O(1) when the returned list is excluded. A different library sort may use O(log n) stack or O(n) temporary storage; that would be a different declared cost model, not an alias for this answer. If the input is already start-sorted, the sorting term disappears and the scan takes O(n) time.

feedback.reason: The O(n log n) in-place heapsort dominates the linear scan, and the declared sort plus active merge state uses O(1) auxiliary space.
